title: Average-case optimality of standard Shellsort
formal: Does there exist a choice, for every \(n\ge2\), of a finite deterministic increment list \(h^{(n)}=(h_1,\ldots,h_p)\), with \(1\le h_i<n\) and \(h_p=1\), such that standard Shellsort with these increments uses at most \(Cn\log n\) key comparisons on average over a uniformly random permutation of \([n]\), for one absolute constant \(C\)? The list may depend on \(n\) but not on the input permutation.
definitions:
The array has positions \(0,\ldots,n-1\) and contains distinct keys of ranks \(1,\ldots,n\). At a pass with increment \(h\), split positions into residue classes modulo \(h\). In each residue class, process entries from left to right by ordinary insertion sort: compare the key being inserted with preceding keys, shift larger keys one position right in that subsequence, and stop at the first preceding key no larger than it or at the beginning. Count every actual comparison between two keys, including the final unsuccessful comparison when it occurs. Index and loop-bound tests are not key comparisons.

Passes execute in the prescribed order. The terminal increment one guarantees sorting for every input. The definition permits any fixed list of valid increments, not an input-dependent choice or randomized compare-exchange pattern. No monotone-decreasing restriction is silently added to the imported question. A sequence with redundant passes still pays for all their comparisons.

Let \(C(h,\pi)\) be the total number of key comparisons on permutation \(\pi\). The requested bound is \(n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}C(h^{(n)},\pi)\le Cn\log n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\); changing the logarithm base changes only the constant. This is a comparison-count existence question, with increments prescribed independently for each size. It imposes no separate bound on computing or describing those increments, and does not claim an overall RAM-time bound that includes generating them.

The input distribution is uniform over all rank permutations, not a random gap list or independent continuous key magnitudes with ties. Average-case success here is a bound on work: standard Shellsort still sorts every permutation exactly.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a family of increment lists exists and has the stated uniform expectation bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation. A randomized modification of Shellsort, a bound on a restricted input distribution, or empirical comparison counts do not settle this deterministic-increment question. A lower bound for a single proposed sequence does not exclude all families.
context:
Goodrich explicitly describes traditional Shellsort as insertion sorting the residue classes of a fixed sequence of offsets. His randomized variant attains near-optimal sorting complexity, but changes the algorithm being analyzed.

Sedgewick lists the average-comparison question for standard Shellsort separately from solved worst-case and randomized-variant questions. The distinction is essential: a difficult worst-case input need not force a large uniform average.

The 2026 preprint studies worst-case lower bounds for specific gap classes, including a geometric-sequence regime. Its abstract does not claim a general average-case impossibility theorem.
why: This would determine whether the original increment-based sorting method can be average-case optimal.

import_provenance.original_statement: Is there a fixed, n-dependent increment sequence for standard Shellsort whose expected number of comparisons is O(n log n) on a uniformly random input permutation? Here each increment means fully insertion-sorting the corresponding residue-class subsequences.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: Goodrich's randomized Shellsort and later Zig-zag Sort already attain O(n log n) for different procedures; they do not settle this standard-Shellsort question. The selection is a historical open problem connected to his work, not an assertion of current activity.

sentences: Standard Shellsort repeatedly insertion sorts positions separated by fixed gaps.
The gap list may depend on array length but is chosen before seeing the input.
The question asks for an O(n log n) expected comparison bound on uniform random permutations.
Randomized variants and lower bounds for specific worst-case gap sequences address different targets.
A resolution would settle a longstanding average-case question for a simple classical sorting algorithm.
